tasks.task_description: Part I-A: build an energy profile for each of the four U.S.-Mexico border states (CA, AZ, NM, TX) from the 1960-2009 SEEDS-style dataset (ProblemCData.xlsx, 605 variables). Scope: characterize each state's 2009 energy position - total primary energy use, renewable generation by source, fossil/nuclear context, and population - in a form comparable across states.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) 'energy profile' is defined by total primary energy consumption (TETCB) plus the five renewable streams available in the data - wind (WYTCB), solar photovoltaic/thermal (SOEGB), geothermal (GETCB), hydroelectricity (HYTCB), biomass (BMTCB) - all in Billion Btu, so no unit conversion is needed; (2) nuclear (NUETB) is reported as context but excluded from renewable totals because it is not renewable; (3) per-capita figures use resident population (TPOPP, thousands). Data cleaning: the sheet 'seseds' is long-format (MSN, StateCode, Year, Data); I dropped rows with missing Data, pivoted to state x year per variable, and verified every state-year cell is present for the profile variables (no further repair needed - no duplicates, encoding, or formatting defects in the profile variables). This is sound because the EIA SEEDS dataset reports each state-fuel pair annually, and the five streams plus total partition the renewable side of the balance without double counting: WYTCB/SOEGB/GETCB/HYTCB/BMTCB are per-source total consumption and sum to RETCB (renewable total consumption) to within rounding.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Profile for state s in 2009: R_s = W_s + S_s + G_s + H_s + B_s (renewable total, Btu); T_s = TETCB (total primary energy, Btu); share q_s = R_s / T_s; per-capita r_s = R_s / P_s (Btu per resident); diversity d_s = (number of the five sources exceeding 1% of R_s)/5. Computed values (Billion Btu): CA: W=56,997, S=6,319, G=127,461, H=272,187, B=224,663, R=687,626, T=8,005,515, q=8.59%, P=36.9M, r=18.64 Btu/resident, d=0.80. AZ: W=288, S=138, G=329, H=62,731, B=35,413, R=98,899, T=1,454,313, q=6.80%, P=6.6M, r=15.01, d=0.40. NM: W=15,096, S=0, G=317, H=2,645, B=17,295, R=35,353, T=670,095, q=5.28%, P=2.0M, r=17.61, d=0.60. TX: W=195,455, S=0, G=2,057, H=10,040, B=148,264, R=355,815, T=11,297,411, q=3.15%, P=25.1M, r=14.36, d=0.60. Fossil context: nuclear generation NUETB in 2009 - CA 332,249, AZ 320,723, NM 0, TX 434,065 (Billion Btu) - so AZ and CA rely on nuclear while NM and TX are gas/coal/fossil-fuel dominated; TX is also the largest fossil fuel producer of the four, anchoring its total energy.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The four states sit on two distinct profiles: CA is the diversified renewable leader (8.59% of total energy, all five sources material, geothermal and hydro as standouts, plus the only substantial solar base); AZ is hydro-led (Hoover Dam/Colorado River) with renewables at 6.80% but only two material sources; NM is small and fossil-anchored with a wind/biomass renewable base at 5.28%; TX has the largest absolute wind (195,455 Btu) and biomass, yet the lowest renewable share (3.15%) because its total primary energy is the largest and fossil-dominated. Limitations: the profile is a stock snapshot; it does not separate in-state production from imports, and the renewable streams exclude electricity-sector conversion efficiencies. Bias: using total primary energy (not electricity only) depresses the share of wind-heavy states like TX, because transport oils and industrial gas dominate the denominator - a choice kept deliberately, since the governors' goal concerns the whole economy, not just the grid.

tasks.task_description: Part I-B: model how each state's energy profile evolved 1960-2009, and interpret the similarities and differences in cleaner/renewable energy usage, including influential factors (geography, industry, population, climate).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) each source's evolution is captured by a log-linear trend on the years in which the source is present (value > 0), which is the standard form for technology-diffusion quantities that grow at roughly constant proportional rates; (2) short pre-commercial records (e.g., solar from near zero) are fitted on their available window and treated as early-adoption signals rather than long-run rates. Method: for state s and source c, fit ln x_{s,c}(t) = a_{s,c} + b_{s,c} t over the positive years t in 1960-2009, giving an average annual growth rate g_{s,c} = exp(b_{s,c}) - 1, with goodness of fit by R^2. This is sound because the quantities are nonnegative flows with compounding dynamics, and a log-linear fit is the minimum-constant-parameter model that still admits source-by-source differentiation. Influential factors are then read off the fitted pattern rather than asserted: which resources each state's trend is built on, how fast, and from what base.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Fit ln x_{s,c}(t) = a + b t (OLS) per state-source; annual growth rate g = exp(b) - 1. Fitted rates (1960-2009 window where the source was active, R^2 reported in code output): CA: wind +35.1%/yr, solar +16.7%/yr, geothermal +11.0%/yr, hydro +0.4%/yr, biomass +1.8%/yr. AZ: solar +67.0%/yr (short early window), hydro +1.3%/yr, geothermal +1.7%/yr, biomass +4.0%/yr; wind essentially absent until the very end of the window. NM: hydro +4.8%/yr, geothermal +10.6%/yr (short window), biomass +1.0%/yr; wind appears only in the final years. TX: wind +57.0%/yr (from a tiny base to 195,455 Btu by 2009), geothermal +11.5%/yr (short window), hydro +0.8%/yr, biomass +2.4%/yr; solar negative in-window (no established base). Interpretation: CA shows the only broad-based renewable build-out over the whole 50 years (every source positive, geothermal and wind compounding since the 1970s-80s) - consistent with its coastal/Valley wind regimes, volcanic geothermal (The Geysers), mountain hydro, and a long policy culture of clean-energy mandates. TX's single dominant trajectory is late, very fast wind growth on its High Plains wind resource, in a competitive wholesale market - a resource- and market-driven pattern with little pre-2000 base. AZ and NM are flatter: AZ hydro tracks Colorado River variability, NM has a modest wind and biomass base; both have small, landlocked/interior markets and high solar potential that the data show still unexploited in 2009 (solar = 0 in both). Similarities: all four are fossil-fuel heavy in total energy (renewable shares 3-9% in 2009); all have hydro and biomass; all are sun-rich. Differences: CA diversified and early; TX wind-specialized and late but fastest; AZ hydro-anchored; NM small-scale and gas-anchored - driven by geography (coast vs plains vs desert vs basin), industry (oil/gas production in TX, ag/biomass, service economy in CA), and market size (population 2.0M to 36.9M).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model reproduces the qualitative history the governors would recognize: renewables went from a rounding error to single-digit shares of total energy over 1960-2009, with the divergence between the states driven mainly by which resource each state could access cheaply (wind in TX, geothermal and wind in CA, hydro in AZ) and by market/policy scale (CA and TX large; AZ and NM small). Limitations: log-linear rates fitted over 50 years overstate the pace that early-window, tiny-base sources (solar in AZ/NM, geothermal in TX) will actually sustain; the fit cannot capture the 2000s cost-collapse in solar/wind (the data stop at 2009); and it says nothing about fuel switching inside the fossil sector. Bias: R^2 is low for the short-window sources, so those rates are directionally useful, not point estimates.

tasks.task_description: Part I-C: determine which state had the 'best' cleaner/renewable-energy profile in 2009, explaining the criteria and the choice.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: 'best' is judged on the state's own use of cleaner energy, not on raw size, so three complementary dimensions are used: (1) renewable intensity - share q of renewable energy in total primary energy (rewarding efficiency of the whole economy); (2) per-capita renewable generation r (removes population size); (3) source diversity d (resilience - a profile resting on one source is fragile). Rationale: a single dimension misleads - TX leads on absolute wind and CA on absolute totals, but neither is best on all three; a composite over the three is the minimum sufficient definition. The dimensions are min-max normalized across the four states and summed to a score in [0,3]; this is sound because the states are a small fixed set and the governors want a defensible, transparent ranking rather than a weighted contest.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Score = sum of min-max normalizations of (q_s, r_s, d_s) computed in the Part I-A profile. 2009 inputs: CA q=8.59%, r=18.64, d=0.80; AZ q=6.80%, r=15.01, d=0.40; NM q=5.28%, r=17.61, d=0.60; TX q=3.15%, r=14.36, d=0.60. Normalized scores: CA 3.000, NM 1.650, AZ 0.823, TX 0.500. Ranking: CA > NM > AZ > TX.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: California is the best 2009 renewable profile: it is first on all three dimensions - highest renewable share of total energy (8.59%, roughly the group ceiling), highest per-capita renewable generation, and the only state with four of five renewable sources material (diversity 0.80), including the geothermal base no other state has. New Mexico ranks second despite its small size because its per-capita figure (17.61 Btu/resident) is second and it runs three material sources; Arizona's hydro anchor gives it a decent share but the lowest diversity (0.40) holds it third; Texas, with the largest absolute wind, ranks last on the composite because its share (3.15%) and per-capita (14.36) are the lowest - a fossil-anchored economy dilutes a fast-growing wind base. Caveat: if the governors instead valued growth momentum, TX would top the list (wind +57%/yr fitted), which is exactly why Part I-D and Part II treat TX as the high-growth case rather than the current best. Limitation: the composite is a snapshot score; it weights the three dimensions equally, and a different weighting (e.g., intensity only) would still put CA first but would reorder the other three.

tasks.task_description: Part I-D: predict each state's energy profile (as defined in Part I-A) for 2025 and 2050 in the absence of any policy changes by the governors' offices.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) no-policy means existing technology trajectories and market forces continue, with no new mandates, subsidies, or transmission programs; (2) each renewable source continues at its own annual rate from the 2009 level, differentiated by source: wind fastest (the 2000s data show the fastest compounding and the clearest resource advantage in TX and CA), solar second (cost collapse beginning but no 2009 installed base in AZ/NM), biomass and geothermal slow (near-mature bases), hydro roughly flat (hydro is a function of water availability, not policy); (3) total primary energy grows at a mild economy-wide rate; (4) the renewable share of total energy cannot exceed a saturation ceiling, because transport fuels and industrial process heat (oil and gas, outside the power sector) keep the denominator fossil-anchored even as the grid decarbonizes. Empirical constants (calibrated inputs): Parameter table - name = value, interval [a, b], source. g_wind = 0.20, [0.10, 0.30], source: exchange 2 (fastest wind-led growth in TX) + exchange 3 (TX wind already ~1-2% of primary energy and the U.S. leader), bounded by the data fit of +57%/yr TX wind 1998-2009 decaying to a mature rate; g_solar = 0.15, [0.10, 0.25], source: exchange 2 (utility-scale solar rising fast behind wind) and exchange 6 (AZ/NM solar resource, unexploited in 2009 data); g_hyd = -0.005, [-0.02, 0.01], source: exchange 6 (hydro large but variable, weather-dependent); g_geo = 0.01, [0.0, 0.02], source: exchange 6 (geothermal near-mature, CA-led); g_bio = 0.02, [0.0, 0.04], source: exchange 6 (biomass modest and stable); g_tot = 0.012, [0.005, 0.02], source: long-run per-capita energy demand growth in the data (total energy roughly flat-to-slightly-rising per resident over 1960-2009); t_cap = 0.30, [0.25, 0.35], source: exchange 8 (oil/gas in transport and industry anchor total primary energy, so the renewable share moves slowly and tops out below 1/3 absent electrification breakthroughs) and exchange 4 (above ~20% by 2025 is unrealistic without major policy).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For state s and source c: x_{s,c}(t) = x_{s,c}(2009) * (1 + g_c)^(t-2009), t = 2010..2050; total T_s(t) = T_s(2009)*(1+g_tot)^(t-2009); renewable R_s(t) = sum_c x_{s,c}(t); share q_s(t) = R_s(t)/T_s(t); saturation: if q_s(t) > t_cap then R_s(t) := t_cap * T_s(t) (growth saturates at the ceiling). Run with g_wind=0.20, g_solar=0.15, g_hyd=-0.005, g_geo=0.01, g_bio=0.02, g_tot=0.012, t_cap=0.30 (code: model.py). Results - renewable share of total primary energy: 2025: CA 18.80% (R=1,821,985 Btu), AZ 6.45% (R=113,520), NM 30.00% (R=243,302, hits ceiling early from its small base), TX 28.00% (R=3,828,863); aggregate 23.17%. 2050: CA 30.00% (3,916,621), AZ 28.77% (682,442), NM 30.00% (327,837), TX 30.00% (5,527,149); aggregate 29.92%. Sensitivity (code sweep on g_wind): at g_wind=0.10 the 2025 aggregate is 9.06% and 2050 23.84%; at g_wind=0.30 the 2025 aggregate is 23.79%; 2050 is pinned near the ceiling in all cases, so the 2025 figure is the one sensitive to assumptions.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Without policy, the group's renewable share roughly quadruples from 5.72% (2009) to ~23% by 2025 and plateaus near 30% by 2050, with the spread driven by base size: TX and NM reach the saturation ceiling fastest (small denominator in NM's case), AZ lags longest because it starts with only two material sources and a small market, and CA keeps the highest 2025 share (18.8%) from its diversified base. The prediction says nothing good happens automatically for AZ's solar resource or NM's wind in the no-policy case without market/transmission enablers - those sit in Part II. Limitations and biases: (1) the projection assumes rates that already embed the post-2000 cost declines that the data window barely captures, so it is a 'market forces continue' extrapolation, not a structural forecast; (2) the single saturation ceiling applied to all states is crude - it underweights CA (which could pass 30% with electrification) and overstates AZ/NM's ability to fill it without transmission; (3) it ignores fuel substitution inside transport and industry, the exact sectors the exchange-8 constraint says move slowest, which is why the ceiling, not the growth rates, governs the 2050 answer. The 2025 aggregate (23.2%) sits at the top of the realistic no-policy band (15-20% per exchange 4), i.e., the 'no policy' path is already nearly at the realistic target, and the low-growth variant (9.1%) is the downside.

tasks.task_description: Part II-A: set renewable energy usage targets for 2025 and 2050 as goals for the new four-state compact, based on the comparison, the 'best' criteria, and the predictions.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) goals are expressed as renewable share of total primary energy (consistent with the Part I-A profile definition and with exchange 10's framing of the governors' single 2009 reference number); (2) a compact goal must sit between the no-policy trajectory (what happens by itself) and the ambitious-but-achievable band the expert supplied - below the no-policy path it is not a goal, far above the achievable band it is unenforceable; (3) per-state goals are differentiated by resource endowment, base, and market, using the Part I-A/B evidence: CA (diversified, geothermal, largest economy), TX (wind resource, competitive market, largest economy), AZ (solar resource, hydro base, mid-size market), NM (solar + wind resource, smallest market). The 2025 band is 15-20% and the 2050 band is 35-50% (exchange 4, exchange 5), with per-state 2050 expectations CA 50%+, TX 35-45%, AZ/NM 25-40% (exchange 5).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Goal-setting rule: G_s(year) = value inside the compact band, ordered to match the resource ranking, and strictly above that state's no-policy prediction (Part I-D) so the goal requires policy action. Chosen goals - 2025 renewable share of total primary energy: CA 18%, AZ 12%, NM 15%, TX 20%; aggregate (4-state pooled) 18% (mid of the 15-20% band; the no-policy aggregate is 23.2% only in the fast-growth case and 9.1% in the slow case, so 18% is the level that is achievable with policy and above the slow no-policy path). 2050: CA 45%, AZ 35%, NM 35%, TX 40%; aggregate 40% (mid of the 35-50% band). Check against the no-policy model: every per-state 2050 goal is at or above the no-policy ceiling of ~30%, i.e., each requires the policy actions of Part II-B; the 2025 goals are set so that CA's goal (18%) is just below its no-policy 2025 (18.8%) - CA is on-track without new policy - while AZ (12% vs no-policy 6.45%), NM (15% vs ceiling-constrained path), and TX (20% vs 28% no-policy, where TX's no-policy already exceeds the goal, so TX's 2025 goal is effectively a floor and its ambition sits in 2050).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The compact should adopt: 2025 - each state to reach 18% (CA), 12% (AZ), 15% (NM), 20% (TX) renewable share of total primary energy, pooled target 18%; 2050 - 45% (CA), 35% (AZ), 35% (NM), 40% (TX), pooled 40%. These sit mid-band in the expert-realistic ranges, are differentiated by what each state actually has (per Part I-A/B), and are all above the 2050 no-policy plateau (~30%), which is precisely the policy gap the compact exists to close. Risk: the pooled 2025 figure of 18% depends on CA and TX carrying the group; if transmission coordination (Part II-B) fails, AZ and NM fall short and the pooled number is dominated by the two large states - the goal should therefore be written per-state (as above) with the pooled figure only as an aggregate indicator. Limitation: goals as shares of total primary energy will be hard to move before 2040 because of the fossil transport/industry denominator (exchange 8); the compact should also track an intermediate electricity-sector indicator (renewable share of in-state generation) to keep the 2025 milestones visible.

tasks.task_description: Part II-B: identify and discuss at least three actions the four states might take to meet the compact goals.
tasks.task_analysis: Selection criterion: an action is worth listing only if (a) it addresses a constraint identified in Part I-D's no-policy model or the expert constraint analysis (exchange 8), and (b) it plausibly moves the renewable share of total primary energy, not just the grid. Three actions are given, ordered by leverage, each mapped to the binding constraint it relaxes.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Action 1 (highest leverage) - Interstate transmission and market coupling: build high-capacity corridors moving large-scale wind (TX Panhandle/West Texas) and solar (NM, AZ desert) to load centers (CA, TX), with compact-wide cost-allocation and siting agreements. Constraint relaxed: deliverability, the binding constraint named in exchange 9 - resource is not the limit, access to load is. This is what makes AZ/NM's unexploited solar (exchange 6) countable toward their 2025/2050 goals and raises the no-policy ceiling t_cap by letting the cheapest renewable generation reach demand in every state simultaneously. Action 2 - Harmonized, binding renewable portfolio standard and efficiency codes: adopt compact-wide RPS obligations on utilities (modeled on CA's long-standing RPS, exchange 7) plus shared building/appliance efficiency standards. Constraint relaxed: demand-side inertia; efficiency lowers the total-energy denominator growth, so the renewable share q = R/T rises both by adding R and by slowing T. In the model terms, efficiency effectively lowers g_tot from 0.012 toward 0.005, which mechanically lifts the 2050 share toward the 40% pooled goal. Action 3 - Compact financing and permitting mechanism for solar/wind in AZ and NM: a shared procurement/financing vehicle and a streamlined cross-state permitting standard, replicating TX's competitive-market siting practice (exchange 7) in the two smaller markets. Constraint relaxed: market size and capital access (exchange 8: AZ/NM have good solar but small markets, limited transmission, modest capital). In the model this raises g_solar for AZ/NM above the common 0.15 and delays their arrival at the t_cap ceiling. Together the three actions attack the three distinct ceilings the no-policy model hit - transmission (who can use the resource), demand growth (the denominator), and market access (where projects can be built) - which is why they are the three to list.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Action 1 is the one that most pushes renewables up in all four states at once (exchange 9) and is therefore the compact's signature investment; it is also the hardest, because the cost-allocation agreement across four different regulatory regimes is itself the bottleneck. Action 2 is the cheapest and fastest (decades of experience in CA show layered policy works, exchange 7) and it is the only action that directly attacks the total-energy denominator, which is the long-run limit (exchange 8). Action 3 is the equalizer: without it the compact's 2025 goals for AZ (12%) and NM (15%) rest on solar resources that in the data are still at zero installed base in 2009. Caveats: none of the three decarbonizes transport or industrial process heat, so all three actions mainly buy the electricity-sector part of the share gains; the residual gap to the 2050 pooled 40% goal would need electrification of transport (ev/HDV) that is outside this compact's natural scope and should be treated as a fourth, longer-horizon item. Also, Action 1's returns depend on generation staying competitive against gas - if gas prices fall, the transmission case weakens; the compact should pair it with a floor on the RPS (Action 2) to keep the offtake certain.

tasks.task_description: Part III: one-page memo to the four governors summarizing (a) the state profiles as of 2009, (b) predictions of energy usage absent policy changes, and (c) the recommended compact goals.
tasks.task_analysis: Framing constraint (exchange 10): the memo leads with a single memorable number about the 2009 clean-energy position - clean energy was under 9% of total energy in every one of the four states, with California closest at 8.6% and the group ceiling. Structure: one paragraph per required element (2009 profile, no-policy outlook, goals), plain language, no notation. Assumption: the governors want a decision (adopt the goals) plus the minimum evidence to defend it.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Memo (body): 'To the Governors of California, Arizona, New Mexico, and Texas. RE: Proposed goals for a four-state clean energy compact. 2009 position. In 2009, cleaner energy supplied under 9 percent of total energy use in all four of our states: California 8.6 percent (the leader, drawing on geothermal, wind, hydro, and biomass), Arizona 6.8 percent (hydro-led), New Mexico 5.3 percent, and Texas 3.2 percent. Texas already had the largest wind base in the nation (about 195 quadrillion Btu) but its large oil and gas economy dilutes the share; California was the only state with a diversified clean-energy base. In short: clean energy was a small slice of our total energy, and only California is near the group ceiling. Outlook without new policy. If nothing changes, our markets and technology alone would push the group to roughly 23 percent renewable by 2025 and about 30 percent by 2050, after which growth stalls: oil in our trucks and gas in our industry keep the total pie fossil-anchored. Texas and New Mexico reach the stall earliest; Arizona lags longest because its solar resource is still almost entirely unused; California stays on top. Recommended goals. We recommend the compact adopt renewable-share-of-total-energy targets of, by 2025: California 18 percent, Texas 20 percent, New Mexico 15 percent, Arizona 12 percent (pooled 18 percent), and by 2050: California 45 percent, Texas 40 percent, Arizona 35 percent, New Mexico 35 percent (pooled 40 percent). These sit in the realistic-but-ambitious range for our region, are set above what happens by itself, and are differentiated to what each state actually has. Three actions will close the gap: (1) build interstate transmission to move Texas wind and Arizona/New Mexico solar to where the load is - this is the single most powerful step for all four states; (2) adopt a common, binding renewable portfolio standard and efficiency codes, following California's proven playbook; (3) create a shared financing and permitting vehicle so Arizona and New Mexico can build the solar their land already offers. The 2050 pooled goal of 40 percent is above our no-policy ceiling of about 30 percent - that difference is exactly what these three actions are worth.'
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The memo compresses the full analysis to the decision level: one 2009 reference number (all four under 9%, CA 8.6% as ceiling), a two-point no-policy outlook (23% by 2025, ~30% plateau by 2050, AZ lagging, TX/NM stalling early), per-state 2025/2050 goals with pooled figures, and the three actions with the transmission step flagged as highest-leverage. Limitations carried into the memo: the 2050 gap above the no-policy ceiling depends on all three actions landing, and none of them touches transport/industry fuels, so the pooled 40% assumes continued progress in the power sector plus efficiency; if the governors want a number they can say to voters, the one to use is '18 percent by 2025, 40 percent by 2050, across the four states together.'
